ev.quote: LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale

contribution.value: LLM.int8() is a two-part Int8 inference procedure (vector-wise quantization plus mixed-precision decomposition that isolates emergent outlier features in 16-bit) that quantizes transformers up to 175B parameters with no performance loss and halves inference memory.

ev.quote: We develop a procedure for Int8 matrix multiplication for feed-forward and attention projection layers in transformers, which cut the memory needed for inference by half while retaining full precision performance
we evaluate the perplexity of the 8-bit transformer on validation data of the C4 corpus (Raffel et al., 2019)

key_results.value: OPT-13B C4 PPL: FP32=12.45, Int8 absmax=19.08, Int8 vector-wise=16.48, LLM.int8()=12.45 (no degradation)
LLM.int8() preserves zeroshot accuracy from 125M up to 175B OPT, while 8-bit absmax vector-wise degenerates to random performance after 6.7B parameters

ev.quote: LLM.int8() maintains full 16-bit performance as we scale from 125M to 175B parameters. On the other hand, the baseline, 8-bit absmax vector-wise quantization, scales poorly and degenerates into random performance

key_results.value: Removing the about 7 outlier feature dimensions (~0.1% of features) drops top-1 softmax probability from ~40% to ~20% and increases perplexity by 600-1000%

ev.section: 4.2 Measuring the Effect of Outlier Features
ev.quote: If the outliers are removed, the mean top-1 softmax probability is reduced from about 40% to about 20%, and validation perplexity increases by 600-1000% even though there are at most 7 outlier feature dimensions

key_results.value: Phase shift at 6.7B parameters: outliers go from 65% to 100% of layers and 35% to 75% of sequence dimensions, co-occurring with quantization failure

ev.section: 4.2 Measuring the Effect of Outlier Features
ev.quote: the emergence of large magnitude features across all layers of a transformer occurs suddenly between 6B and 6.7B parameters as shown in Figure 3a as the percentage of layers affected increases from 65% to 100%. The number of sequence dimensions affected increases rapidly from 35% to 75%

key_results.value: BLOOM-176B end-to-end per-token latency: bf16 baseline 239 ms (8xA100) vs LLM.int8() 247 ms on only 3xA100 (similar speed, fewer GPUs)

ev.quote: we present the first multi-billion-scale Int8 quantization procedure for transformers that does not incur any performance degradation
a 175B parameter 16/32-bit checkpoint can be loaded, converted to Int8, and used immediately without performance degradation
The **LLM.int8**() method is the combination of absmax vector-wise quantization and mixed precision decomposition
We develop a procedure for Int8 matrix multiplication for feed-forward and attention projection layers in transformers
the small number of large magnitude feature dimensions (≈0.1%) are represented in 16-bit precision while the other 99.9% of values are multiplied in 8-bit

we also include a new mixed-precision decomposition scheme, which isolates the outlier feature dimensions into a 16-bit matrix multiplication while still more than 99.9% of values are multiplied in 8-bit

For vector-wise quantization, matrix multiplication can be seen as a sequence of independent inner products of row and column vectors. As such, we can use a separate quantization normalization constant for each inner product
a 175B parameter 16/32-bit checkpoint can be loaded, converted to Int8, and used immediately without performance degradation
We use NVIDIA A40 GPUs for this evaluation
| Academic server | 8x RTX 3090 | 24 GB | **OPT-175B / BLOOM** | OPT-66B |

value.baseline: FP16 cuBLAS matrix multiplication (175B model dim 12288)
value.hardware: NVIDIA A100 (cuBLASLt Int8 with vector-wise + mixed-precision decomposition)

strengths.value: First Int8 method to preserve full predictive performance for 175B-parameter transformers, including OPT-175B and BLOOM-176B.

ev.quote: we present the first multi-billion-scale Int8 quantization procedure for transformers that does not incur any performance degradation

strengths.value: Halves inference memory and lets BLOOM-176B run on a single consumer GPU server, broadening access for low-resource researchers.

ev.quote: making it possible to use OPT-175B/BLOOM on a single server with consumer GPUs

strengths.value: Provides the first descriptive analysis of emergent outlier features that explains why prior 8-bit methods fail at the 6.7B scale.

ev.section: 4.2 Measuring the Effect of Outlier Features
ev.quote: the emergence of large magnitude features across *all* layers of a transformer occurs suddenly between 6B and 6.7B parameters

strengths.value: Open-source bitsandbytes library and Hugging Face integration, making the method easy to reproduce and apply to existing models.

ev.quote: We open-source our software and release a Hugging Face Transformers (Wolf et al., 2019) integration making our method available to all hosted Hugging Face Models that have linear layers

weaknesses.value: Studied only Int8; the FP8 data type and its potential accuracy or speed gains are left to future work.

ev.quote: our analysis is solely on the Int8 data type, and we do not study 8-bit floating-point (FP8) data types

weaknesses.value: Method is only validated up to 175B parameters; emergent properties at larger scales could break the procedure.

ev.quote: we only study models with up to 175B parameters. While we quantize a 175B model to Int8 without performance degradation, additional emergent properties might disrupt our quantization methods at larger scales

weaknesses.value: Attention function itself is not quantized, limiting compute savings beyond memory bandwidth reduction.

ev.quote: we do not use Int8 multiplication for the attention function

weaknesses.value: Quantization overhead actually slows inference for models smaller than 6.7B parameters compared to FP16.

ev.quote: The quantization overhead can slow inference for models with less than 6.7B parameters, as compared to a FP16 baseline

limitations.value: Tested only on data-centre GPUs (A40, A100) and academic-tier RTX 3090; no mobile or edge-class devices evaluated.

ev.quote: We use NVIDIA A40 GPUs for this evaluation

limitations.value: Safety, bias, refusal, and jailbreak behaviour after quantization are not measured; evaluation is on perplexity and zero-shot tasks.

ev.quote: We develop a procedure for Int8 matrix multiplication for feed-forward and attention projection layers in transformers, which cut the memory needed for inference by half while retaining full precision performance

limitations.value: Bit-widths below 8 are not explored for these multi-billion models.

ev.quote: we focus on 8-bit transformers that *do not* degrade performance and that can benefit from commonly used GPUs that accelerates inference through Int8 tensor cores

limitations.value: Training and finetuning at scale with Int8 is not solved; appendix shows attention-layer Int8 training degrades performance.

ev.quote: we focus on inference but do not study training or finetuning

future_work_stated.value: Extend the analysis to 8-bit floating-point (FP8) data types once GPU/TPU support exists.

ev.quote: Since current GPUs and TPUs do not support this data type, we believe this is best left for future work. However, we also believe many insights from Int8 data types will directly translate to FP8 data types

future_work_stated.value: Develop additional quantization methods for the attention function itself, beyond linear projections.

ev.quote: an initial exploration of this problem indicated that a solution required additional quantization methods beyond those we developed here, and we leave this for future work

future_work_stated.value: Tackle Int8 training at scale, balancing quantization precision, training speed, and engineering complexity.

ev.quote: Int8 training at scale requires complex trade-offs between quantization precision, training speed, and engineering complexity and represents a very difficult problem. We again leave this to future work
Did you report error bars (e.g., with respect to the random seed after running experiments multiple times)? [No] Our experiments are deterministic for each model
We also report the *per-token* generation speed in milliseconds for different batch sizes
We open-source our software and release a Hugging Face Transformers (Wolf et al., 2019) integration
